opus-5.5.text:
Well, the first thing I learned is that arguments alone don't move people very much. When I started speaking publicly about catastrophic risks, I thought that if I laid out the reasoning carefully, people would follow it. It doesn't work that way. People have strong psychological defenses against ideas that threaten their sense of the future or their identity. And I include myself in that. For years I didn't take these risks seriously, even though I'd heard the arguments. I was invested in the idea that my work was good for humanity, and it's uncomfortable to consider that the thing you've devoted your life to could contribute to something terrible.

What changed it for me wasn't a new argument. It was the experience of ChatGPT and realizing that the timeline was much shorter than I'd assumed. And then thinking about my children, my grandson, and asking what world they would live in in ten or twenty years. That emotional connection made me willing to look at arguments I had brushed aside.

So one lesson is to meet people where they are. Rather than starting with extinction scenarios, which many people find too abstract or too much like science fiction, it often helps to start with things they can already see: systems that deceive, that pursue goals in ways we didn't intend, that resist being shut down in experiments. These aren't hypothetical anymore. We have empirical evidence of these behaviors, and that's much harder to dismiss.

Another lesson is humility. I try not to say "this will happen." I say we don't know, and that's exactly the problem. If even a few percent of serious researchers think there's a meaningful chance of catastrophe, that's not acceptable when what's at stake is so large. We wouldn't accept that for a bridge or an airplane or a drug. The precautionary argument resonates with a lot of people who aren't convinced by any particular scenario.

I've also learned not to demonize the other side. Many colleagues who disagree with me are sincere and thoughtful. Some of it is honest disagreement about the science, and some of it, frankly, is the same motivated reasoning I had. Respecting people while challenging them keeps the conversation going. Making it tribal shuts it down.

Finally, it matters who delivers the message. When people who built the technology say "I'm worried," it carries weight that outsiders' warnings sometimes don't. I think that's part of why Geoff Hinton and I speaking up has had some effect. It gives others, including policymakers, permission to take this seriously without feeling they're being alarmist. But we need many more voices: scientists, yes, but also people from civil society and from many countries, because these risks concern everyone, not just the handful of companies and governments racing ahead.

r001.rationale: The response says arguments alone often fail because of psychological defenses, but it does not address brief public messaging or beliefs about humans and machines.

r002.rationale: It recommends starting with observable AI behaviors people can recognize, but does not say this is needed to capture attention through brief public messaging.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss regulation or warn that responses to immediate concerns could leave more serious AI risks unaddressed.

r004.rationale: It recommends respectful conversation, but does not identify extended, nearly one-on-one dialogue as an effective way to challenge preconceived beliefs.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I learned is humility, because I was one of the people who didn't take it seriously for a very long time. For decades I was working on deep learning thinking that human-level AI was so far away that these questions were almost philosophical, something for the next generation to worry about. And then ChatGPT came out and I had to confront the fact that my own timelines had been wrong, maybe by a lot. So when I talk to colleagues who are dismissive, I don't come at it as someone who always saw this coming. I come at it as someone who changed his mind, and I try to explain what moved me, because I think that's more persuasive than lecturing.

The second thing is that the resistance is rarely about the arguments. When I would sit down with people and go through the technical reasons why loss of control or misuse could happen, very often they would concede each step, and yet at the end they would still say, "but it won't happen." And I came to realize this is something psychological. We're talking about things that are frightening and also uncertain, and the mind has many ways of protecting itself from that combination. There's a kind of motivated reasoning that we all do, including me. If you have spent your career building these systems, if your identity and your salary and your sense of doing good in the world are tied to this technology, it is very hard to look at the possibility that you might be contributing to something catastrophic. So I try to be gentle about it and to say, look, I understand, I was in the same position.

The third thing is that the probabilities matter less than people think. I spent a lot of energy early on arguing about whether the risk is one percent or ten percent or fifty percent. But that's a distraction. What I say now is: even if you think the probability is small, when the stakes include the fate of humanity, we don't normally accept that kind of gamble. We don't let a company build a nuclear reactor in the middle of a city because they are pretty confident it won't melt down. We ask for evidence of safety. So I try to shift the conversation from "are you sure this will happen" to "can you demonstrate that it won't," because that's the standard we apply to every other dangerous technology.

And finally, I learned that you have to speak to people in the language that connects to what they already care about. For scientists, it's the technical uncertainty, the fact that we really don't know how to align these systems or even to interpret them. For governments, it's national security, it's the concentration of power, it's the democratic question of who decides. For the public, it's often more concrete things, jobs, manipulation, their children. These are all legitimate concerns and they are all connected, so I don't think we should be choosing between the near-term harms and the catastrophic ones. They come from the same root, which is that we are building systems more and more capable without the understanding or the governance to keep them under control.

I'll say also that there's a role for emotion. For a long time I thought I should stay very rational and detached. But what actually changed me was thinking about my children and my grandchildren, and asking what kind of world they would live in. When I started talking about that openly, I found people responded much more honestly. So I don't hide it anymore. It's not a weakness in the argument. It's the reason the argument matters.

astra-6.text:
I think one thing I’ve learned is that explaining the technical arguments is only part of the job. You also have to listen to why someone finds the conclusion difficult to accept. They might be excited about the benefits of AI. They might worry that talking about catastrophic risks will distract from harms that are already happening. Those are concerns you have to engage with seriously.

And we should be very clear about uncertainty. We don’t know how quickly these systems will become more capable, or whether particular scenarios will happen. But uncertainty is not a reason to assume that everything will be fine. The important question is: given what we don’t know, and given how large the consequences could be, what precautions make sense?

I also think it helps to give people something constructive to do. If the message is only frightening, people can turn away. If you explain that there are research questions we can work on and decisions we can make to reduce the risk, then it becomes a problem we can address together.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one thing is that simply presenting a frightening scenario is not enough. People need to understand why you think it is plausible, where the uncertainty is, and what we can actually do about it. Otherwise, the reaction can be to push it away, because it feels overwhelming.

And different people have different concerns. Some are focused on harms that are already happening; others are thinking about losing control of much more capable systems. I think we should resist turning that into a competition. We can care about both.

What I try to emphasize is that we don’t need certainty about a catastrophe to take precautions. We need to ask whether the risk is sufficiently serious, and whether there are reasonable measures that could reduce it. That’s a much more useful conversation than asking people to agree with every prediction about the future.
